title: When would you choose AWS Lambda over a container (ECS/EKS), and what are Lambda's constraints (cold starts, max execution time, memory/CPU coupling, statelessness)?
shortTitle: When to Choose Lambda Over a Container, and Lambda's Constraints
keyPoints: Choose Lambda for short-lived, event-driven, spiky work that scales to zero and bills per millisecond with no server management.
Keep containers for long-running, steady, latency-sensitive, or heavy workloads that exceed Lambda's limits.
Cold starts add initialization latency when Lambda spins up a fresh execution environment, especially for Java due to JVM startup.
Lambda has a maximum execution time of fifteen minutes; longer tasks must use containers or Step Functions.
Memory and CPU are coupled: you set memory and CPU scales proportionally, so a CPU-bound function may need extra memory just to get more CPU.
Lambda is stateless: no reliable local state persists between invocations, so state must go to DynamoDB, S3, or a cache.

s1_definition.oneliner: Choose Lambda for short, event-driven, spiky work that scales to zero, but respect its cold starts, fifteen-minute limit, memory-coupled CPU, and statelessness; keep containers for long-running, steady, or heavy workloads.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **AWS Lambda** – a serverless compute service that runs code only on invocation, scales automatically from zero to thousands of concurrent executions, and bills per millisecond.
- **Cold start** – the added latency when Lambda initializes a new execution environment (downloading code, starting the runtime, running init code).
- **Maximum execution time** – fifteen minutes; functions that exceed this must be containers or be broken into Step Functions steps.
- **Memory-CPU coupling** – you configure memory (128 MB to 10 GB) and CPU scales proportionally; you cannot set CPU independently.
- **Statelessness** – each invocation may run in a different environment with no reliable local state; external stores are required.
- **Provisioned concurrency** – pre-warms a specified number of environments to eliminate cold starts for latency-sensitive paths.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of two ways to staff a desk at National Bank of India. A container is a clerk who sits at the desk all day, ready instantly -- great if customers come constantly, but you pay the clerk even when no one shows up. Lambda is an on-call clerk who only walks in when a specific form arrives, handles it, and leaves -- you pay only for those minutes, but there is a short wait while the clerk walks in (the cold start), the clerk must finish within a strict time limit, cannot keep personal notes between visits (statelessness), and to give the clerk a faster brain you also have to give them a bigger desk (memory and CPU are tied).

  │  Lambda   │                │  Container   │
  │           │                │  (ECS/EKS)   │

  │ Pay/ms    │                │ No time limit│

  └──────────┘                └──────────────┘


          Cold Start vs Warm Invocation

  Cold Start:
  ┌──────────────┬────────────────┬────────────┬─────────────┐
  │ Download code│ Start runtime  │ Static init│ Handle req  │
  │              │ (JVM for Java) │            │             │
  └──────────────┴────────────────┴────────────┴─────────────┘
  |<---------- cold start latency ----------->|<-- fast --->|

  Warm Invocation:
  ┌─────────────┐
  │ Handle req  │  Environment reused, no init
  └─────────────┘
  |<-- fast --->|

sections.s6_takeaway:
I choose AWS Lambda over a container when the workload is genuinely event-driven, short-lived, and spiky or infrequent, because Lambda runs only when an event arrives, scales automatically from zero to thousands of concurrent executions, and bills per millisecond, costing nothing when idle. I keep the workload on a container in ECS or EKS when it is long-running, steady, latency-sensitive in a way cold starts would hurt, or exceeds Lambda's limits.

The four constraints I always weigh are cold starts, the fifteen-minute limit, memory-CPU coupling, and statelessness. Cold starts add initialization latency when Lambda spins up a fresh environment, which is worse for Java; I mitigate with init outside the handler, provisioned concurrency, and SnapStart. The fifteen-minute limit means anything longer needs a container or Step Functions. Memory and CPU are coupled, so a CPU-bound function sometimes gets extra memory purely for CPU. And Lambda is stateless: each invocation may run in a different environment, so state goes to DynamoDB, S3, or a cache.

Beyond the core constraints, there are limits on payload size, package size, and concurrency that shape what fits on Lambda versus what belongs on a container.

At National Bank of India I ran the statement-PDF indexer as a Lambda because it fires a few hundred times a day in bursts and costs nothing between runs. I kept the transfer API on ECS Fargate because it serves steady traffic all day and cannot afford cold-start latency. The nightly reconciliation job, which runs about forty minutes, could not be a single Lambda because of the fifteen-minute limit, so I ran it as an ECS task orchestrated by Step Functions.

Remember one sentence: choose Lambda for short, event-driven, spiky work that scales to zero, and keep containers for long-running, steady, or heavy workloads that exceed Lambda's fifteen-minute limit or need predictable latency.
